content_html:
Plasticity → Memory Cycle

Neuroplasticity drives the lifecycle of memory: encoding new experiences, stabilizing them in storage, reactivating and updating them during recall (reconstruction and reconsolidation), and flexibly recombining details to simulate possible futures. Each stage modifies synaptic and circuit properties, making memory an inherently constructive and adaptive process.

Plasticity: Activity-dependent changes at synapses and circuits (e.g., LTP/LTD) prepare networks to encode experience.
Encoding: Co-active neurons strengthen their connections; patterns of potentiated synapses constitute engrams.
Storage: Over hours–days, molecular and structural consolidation stabilizes traces; sleep and replay support systems consolidation.
Recall / Reconstruction: Reactivation retrieves memories but also renders them labile; reconsolidation can update content.
Future Simulation: Episodic fragments are recombined to imagine plausible futures; this reuse of memory supports planning.
